explanations.answer: Gazing with desire at a virgin
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Job says, “How then could I gaze with desire at a virgin?” A covenant is a serious promise, and he made this one with his own eyes. I can't even make a promise to my eyes about a cooling rack full of fresh cookies, so this man is playing in a different league.

explanations.answer: Glaring at the men who mock him
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd think so, friend, because men were mocking him right before this (Job 30:1). But the covenant isn't about glaring at anybody. Job says it keeps him from gazing with desire at a virgin. Different promise, different problem.

explanations.answer: Weeping over all he has lost
explanations.explanation: Job has lost a lot, and I'd never tell a man not to cry. But this covenant isn't about tears. Job says it's about not gazing with desire at a virgin. His eyes made a promise, and weeping wasn't part of it.

Not quite, baker. Job asks, “Does He not see my ways and count my every step?” That's a man who believes God IS watching. He isn't saying God looks away. He's saying God sees every step, and he's fine with that.

Right, baker. Job says, “Does He not see my ways and count my every step?” He isn't complaining that God is distracted. He says God sees his ways and counts every step. That's a man who's not worried about being watched.

That's the one, friend. Job says, “let God weigh me with honest scales, that He may know my integrity.” Honest scales means no thumb on the side. Job wants God to weigh the whole thing and see what's there.

Job has plenty of sorrow, baker, and he's talked about it before. But that's not what he puts on the scales here. He says, “let God weigh me with honest scales, that He may know my integrity.” He's asking God to look at his integrity.

Close to a topic Job brings up later, friend. Further down he asks what if he trusted in gold (Job 31:24). But on the scales in verse 6, he's asking God to know his integrity. The scales weigh the man, not the money.

Right, baker. Every one of those “if I did this” lines is Job putting a promise behind his claim that he didn't. He's basically saying, if I did that, then let this happen to me. It's a long list of big promises. A man who says that is putting his name behind his innocence.

I get the thought, friend, but listen to the shape of it. Job says things like “If I have walked in falsehood…” and then names what should happen to him. He's saying he didn't do those things, not that he did. That's no confession.

No forgiveness request in these verses, baker. Job lays out what trouble should come to him IF he did these things. That's how someone talks when he's insisting he didn't do them. He's standing on his innocence, not asking for a pardon.
Yes, baker. Job calls it “a heinous crime, an iniquity to be judged.” He doesn't use soft words here. He says plainly that being enticed by his neighbor's wife would be serious.
A mistake is a spilled bowl of flour, friend. Job uses a much heavier word. He says it would be “a heinous crime, an iniquity to be judged.” He treats it as serious.

Job does talk about secrets later in this chapter, baker. But in verse 11 the word he uses is “crime.” He says it would be “a heinous crime, an iniquity to be judged.” That's a heavy thing, and he says it plainly.
Right, baker. Job says it's a fire that “burns down to Abaddon” and “would root out my entire harvest.” That's a fire that takes everything he's worked for. He doesn't see this as a small thing.
A good name is a fair guess, friend, but it isn't what Job says. He says the fire “would root out my entire harvest.” The fire reaches down to Abaddon and takes the whole harvest.
Job does have flocks, baker. In Job 31:20 he mentions the fleece of his sheep. But the fire in verse 12 “would root out my entire harvest.” The harvest is what he says it takes.

That's it, baker. Job asks, “what will I do when God rises to judge? How will I answer when called to account?” He knows his servants aren't the final word on how he treats them. God is, and Job doesn't want to face that moment with a rejected complaint behind him.

His friends are still in the room, friend, but they aren't who Job names here. He says, “what will I do when God rises to judge?” His worry is about answering to God. Nothing in these verses is about his friends finding out.

The text never says anything about the servants walking away, baker. Job asks, “what will I do when God rises to judge? How will I answer when called to account?” The moment he can't face is God rising to judge.

True, baker. Job asks, “Did not He who made me in the womb also make them? Did not the same One form us in the womb?” The same One made Job and the servants. That's why Job says their complaints are not something to push aside.
It's the other way around, friend. Job says, “Did not He who made me in the womb also make them? Did not the same One form us in the womb?” So the same God formed Job and his servants.

True, baker. Job says, “from my youth I reared him as would a father, and from my mother's womb I guided the widow.” That's a long stretch of caring for people who had no one else. Job says it's been his whole life.

The text says the opposite, friend. Job says, “from my youth I reared him as would a father, and from my mother's womb I guided the widow.” He says he's been doing this since he was young. This isn't new to him.

explanations.answer: He saw he had support in the gate
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Job says, “because I saw that I had support in the gate.” The gate is where the city's business and judging happened. He's describing a man who hurts the fatherless because he thinks the powerful people have his back.

explanations.answer: He saw the child had stolen from him
explanations.explanation: No stealing in this verse, friend. The reason Job names is “because I saw that I had support in the gate.” He doesn't mention the child doing anything at all.

explanations.answer: He saw his friends doing the same
explanations.explanation: Nope, baker, and his friends aren't mentioned here. Job names this reason: “because I saw that I had support in the gate.” It's about having people in power on his side.

explanations.answer: May his arm fall from his shoulder
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Job says, “then may my arm fall from my shoulder and be torn from its socket.” It's a heavy thing to say, and he says it plainly. The arm that would lift against the fatherless is the arm he names.
That's not in this verse, friend. Job says, “then may my arm fall from my shoulder and be torn from its socket.” It's the arm that would lift against the fatherless.
Job doesn't say that, baker. He says, “then may my arm fall from my shoulder and be torn from its socket.” The hand lifted against the fatherless is the one he talks about.
It's the reverse, baker. Job says, “For calamity from God terrifies me, and His splendor I cannot overpower.” He's not acting like he's too tough for God. He says calamity from God terrifies him.
Right, baker. Job says, “For calamity from God terrifies me, and His splendor I cannot overpower.” That's a man who takes God seriously. He says he can't overpower God's splendor.

That's the word, friend. Job says, “if I have rejoiced in my great wealth because my hand had gained so much.” It's the picture of a man patting himself on the back. I know that move, because I do it when a batch comes out pretty.
I see why you'd guess it, baker, but Job doesn't say that. His line is “because my hand had gained so much.” The gain is credited to his own hand.
Flocks are a fair guess, friend, since Job has sheep (Job 31:20). But here the word is “hand.” He says, “because my hand had gained so much.”

explanations.answer: He would have denied God on high
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Job says, “this would also be an iniquity to be judged, for I would have denied God on high.” The sun and moon are beautiful, but Job says giving his heart to them would deny God. His reason is that plain.

explanations.answer: He would have broken a promise to his friends
explanations.explanation: Job doesn't mention a promise to his friends here, baker. He gives his own reason: “for I would have denied God on high.” It's a matter between him and God.

explanations.answer: He would have forgotten the needy
explanations.explanation: The needy came up earlier, friend, in Job 31:19. But the reason Job gives here is “for I would have denied God on high.” He's talking about the sun and the moon, not the poor.

That's it, baker. Job says, “I have not allowed my mouth to sin by asking for his life with a curse.” He can say the words out loud and not be ashamed. A man who keeps his mouth closed on that is doing the hard thing.

Good thinking, friend, because Job does mention his heart in other places in this chapter. But in this verse the word is “mouth.” He says he has not allowed his mouth to sin by asking for his enemy's life with a curse.
Job does talk about his hands in this chapter, baker. But here he's talking about words. He says, “I have not allowed my mouth to sin by asking for his life with a curse.”

Right, baker. Job says, “no stranger had to lodge on the street, for my door has been open to the traveler.” A stranger on the road had a place at his house. I think that's worth more than any sign on a door.
Princes would have had places to stay, friend, and Job doesn't say them here. He says, “my door has been open to the traveler.” He's talking about the stranger with nowhere to go.
Elders aren't who Job names, baker. He says no stranger had to lodge on the street, “for my door has been open to the traveler.” The open door is for the traveler.

That's right, baker. Job says, “because I greatly feared the crowds and the contempt of the clans terrified me, so that I kept silent and would not go outside.” That's a man hiding at home. He's saying he never did that.
Job doesn't say anything about a reward, friend. The reason he names is “because I greatly feared the crowds and the contempt of the clans terrified me.” It's fear that keeps a man inside.
That's a thoughtful guess, baker, but it isn't what the text says. Job says, “because I greatly feared the crowds and the contempt of the clans terrified me.” The reason is fear of the crowds.
It's the opposite, baker. Job says, “Let the Almighty answer me.” He signs his name and then wants God to answer. He's not asking for silence.
Right, friend. Job says, “Here is my signature. Let the Almighty answer me.” He puts his name on it and asks God to answer. A man who wants silence doesn't talk like that.
Yes, baker. Job says, “Surely I would carry it on my shoulder and wear it like a crown.” Most people would hide a list of charges. Job says he'd wear it like a crown.
That's not what Job says, friend. He says, “Surely I would carry it on my shoulder and wear it like a crown.” He keeps the charges close.
Hiding is the opposite of Job's plan, baker. He says, “Surely I would carry it on my shoulder and wear it like a crown.” He wants the charges out in the open.
True, baker. Job says, “I would give account of all my steps…” and says he would approach God like a prince. That's a man who's ready to talk. I think it's a bold way to walk in.
It's true, friend. Job says, “I would give account of all my steps…” and then says he would approach God like a prince. He isn't hiding anything in this picture.

That's it, baker. Job says, “if I have devoured its produce without payment or broken the spirit of its tenants.” Taking from the land and not paying is what he's denying. He's saying he treated the people who worked it fairly.
Thanks is a nice thought, friend, but the word in the verse is “payment.” Job says, “if I have devoured its produce without payment.” He's talking about what the tenants were owed.
Job does care about prayer, baker, but that's not the word in this verse. He says, “if I have devoured its produce without payment or broken the spirit of its tenants.” The missing piece is payment.

Right, baker. Job says, “then let briers grow instead of wheat and stinkweed instead of barley.” The fields he planted would turn into weeds. That's how he ends his list, and then it says the words of Job are done.
No locusts in this verse, friend. Job says, “then let briers grow instead of wheat and stinkweed instead of barley.” The curse is weeds growing where the grain should be.
Floods aren't in the text, baker. Job says, “then let briers grow instead of wheat and stinkweed instead of barley.” The picture is weeds taking over the field.
